option: A: Consolidate in place. Keep the schema and functions, put one authorization core under them, route every check through it, add the authorization matrix test as a CI gate, fix the verified bugs, and finish or delete half-migrations only where they block.
thesis: The foundation is sound. A rebuild would produce the same one again: the API checks the login token with Supabase Auth, then calls *_service(actor) functions that no browser can execute, and the database does the permission check. That pattern is applied everywhere. 135+ API route call sites pass the verified user. 0 of 345 functions that take an actor id can be run by the browser. RLS is on for 158 of 158 tables. 191 of 202 links between organization tables carry workspace_id. The role source had 0 mismatches. The real disease is that one decision ("may this person do this at this location") is written about 12 times in helpers and 51 times inline. It also appears in 45 functions that borrow the logged-in-user slot, 20 route-level checks in the API, and 65 RLS policies. The copies have drifted apart. Nothing ran the database tests in CI, so nobody saw the drift. Every verified defect traces to one of four causes: that duplication, leftover grants, missing CI, or two contained model gaps (the plan-edit lock covers a whole workspace and week; a time-off request carries one location). None traces to the domain model. So the fix is to replace the duplicated rule with one authorize()/scope_set() core, wrapped in an executable matrix and in catalog tests that fail CI whenever the old style reappears. That can be done in place, domain by domain, with RPC shapes kept stable. The 168 web files that read those shapes and the 4,275 test assertions that record decisions already made both survive. The history argues against a rebuild: this repo already is one ("Initial clean rebuild foundation", 90f0fad, 2026-08-18). Its brief prescribed location scope in every check and role test users, and the same failure classes still came back within 5 weeks. The missing piece was enforcement, not a clean slate. Option A adds enforcement and delivers protection within the first 2–4 weeks. A rebuild delivers nothing until it ends.
what_it_fixes: The same rule written in many places: 12 location-scope versions and 6 'may the manager reach this person' versions in helpers, 51 functions with their own inline checks, 45 functions that borrow the logged-in-user slot (set_config) and 20 route-level checks in the API all collapse into one actor_context + authorize() + scope_set(). Copies can no longer disagree.

A manager blocked for missing documents can still edit and publish schedules (E1: acquired an edit session and wrote a shift). Checking document status once, in actor_context, closes both the database and the API route-local paths.

An empty (NULL) location counts as 'anywhere' in 4 helpers, across 56 call sites. E2: a Main Dining manager archived a Garden Room draft. authorize() refuses NULL, and lists are filtered by scope_set.
A suspended workspace still accepts direct writes to some tables (E4). The workspace-status check moves into the single actor resolution step.

The browser can rewrite who belongs to the workspace and with what role (E5b/E6), give a manager a location without a work assignment (E5), link a membership to another organization's employee record, set the workspace to deleted or switch Shift Hub on, create an active workspace, and write fake audit entries. Fix: revoke unused write grants, allow UPDATE on workspaces only for name and logo, and turn the 9 single-column links into composite FKs.

Internal functions that trust a caller-supplied user id are executable by everyone (app_private default-ACL gap, and a revoke lost on drop/recreate). Fix: a default-privilege revoke plus catalog tests that cover public and app_private.

The role class is stored twice with no guard on the roles side. A composite FK (role_id, workspace_id, role) to workspace_roles(id, workspace_id, access_class) makes drift impossible without changing any of the ~76 functions that read either column.
Role-derived facts are not cleaned up when a role changes: stale scope rows and all_locations after a manager is demoted to employee.
The employee permission allowlist exists in 4 copies and the role defaults in 3. Both move to one SQL source.
Important dates are read without a location check (E3). Their read path goes through scope_set.

The plan-edit lock covers a whole workspace and week, so a takeover followed by a save silently deletes another location's draft shifts. Locks, sessions and saves become per location plus week. This is the only data-losing item.

The time-off request carries a single location chosen by the employee. Under M2 D4 the field is removed and approval takes a vote from each affected location. D3 applies to terminate and archive, and rank checks apply to approvals.

The verified BL-070 bugs: saving an employee wipes the approved preferred name; managers cannot terminate (14 Sep regression); the Schedule grid reads the old availability system; approved time off can be softened; preferred-name notifications have no recipients; a swap's source shift is counted as a conflict with itself (BL-092); Shift Hub is switched off with no way to turn it on; owner, admin and manager cannot reach the employee screens.
The database tests are invisible to CI. A database job is added, running the matrix plus a list of green files that only ever grows.

Manager test fixtures describe a manager the product cannot create (hand-inserted scope; the deferred sync never fires under rollback). The matrix world is built through product entry points and ends with 'set constraints all immediate'.

Denials come back in 4 different shapes (42501, NULL, P0002, and a validation error that runs before the scope check), and tests pin message wording. authorize() raises 42501 with a machine-readable key before any validation runs.

Dead or broken leftovers: 8 dead policies, 3 tautology policies, the dev-identity bypass gated in 2 inconsistent ways, public realtime channels, the no-service-key fallback resolver, tombstone functions, and a dead overload that leaks names.
Scheduled exports always fail because the server role cannot read workspaces, workspace_onboarding or workspace_memberships.
what_it_does_not_fix: Kiosk (6 tables) and time tracking (8 tables) stay in the schema. Option A only brings their helpers under authorize() where they are called. Deleting them is a separate decision.
Line Up (11 tables, reds 32–38) keeps its old checks until the simplification decision is made. It sits in the matrix's exempt list, with a reason.

The 319 migrations are not squashed, and the 36 _base wrapper chains are collapsed only where a domain is touched. The migration history stays long, and a reader still meets old layers in untouched areas.
The web stays coupled to the snake_case RPC shapes (439 zod schemas, 3,495 reads in 168 files). Option A deliberately keeps those shapes stable; it does not clean them up.

What screens show can still disagree with what the database allows (64 permission checks and 10 route guards in the web, 31 in the API). The matrix cannot see UI gating unless a later web can() helper is checked against the matrix's expectations.
Eligibility (location + job + availability for swap, cover and release) needs a second matrix on the same engine. The authorization matrix does not cover it.
Fields leaking inside an allowed response (e.g. private contact data), and who receives which notification, beyond the specific preferred-name bug.
Concurrency and lock behaviour beyond the per-location lock change.
The process cause behind both generations: decisions made faster than they are enforced. CI gates close most of it, but a wrong line in expected() is still enforced faithfully.

Hosted configuration facts that were never verified: whether Vercel sets NODE_ENV=production, and which schemas the hosted project exposes. Option A removes the dependency on NODE_ENV but does not check the hosted project.

plan_steps.step: 0. Write down the decisions the matrix's expected() function needs. Scope model M2 ('person shared, shift local'). D1: manager-class roles cannot hold settings.* write permissions. D3: a manager may terminate or archive only when all of the person's locations are in scope; otherwise admin or owner. Approved time off is always hard. BL-091: the new availability system is the one that stays. Shift Hub vs the old Requests flow. Record them in the project conventions file. Assumption: the owner decides in one or two sittings. Anything still open becomes a 'decide:' todo cell rather than a blocker.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Every rule expected() needs is either written down as decided or listed as a named open question. The owner has confirmed the list.

plan_steps.step: 1. Safety net first. (a) Add a CI job: supabase start, then run pgTAP from an allowlist of the currently green files plus the new matrix; the list may only grow. (b) Write supabase/tests/authorization_matrix.test.sql to the design measured in the test-infra investigation. The world has 2 organizations, the Kadikoy and Besiktas locations, and 14 actors, with managers built through their own employee record and 'set constraints all immediate'. It covers about 45 actions, probes each cell with a sentinel exception so every cell sees the same fixture, puts the open decisions in todo cells, adds a consistency layer across the location predicates, and adds a coverage sweep: every actor *_service is listed or exempt with a reason. (c) Add catalog sweeps over public and app_private: no SECURITY DEFINER function with a NULL ACL; only an allowlist of tables writable by authenticated; no TRUNCATE; no policy without a grant. (d) Add an API route-matrix vitest with restricted, suspended and employee contexts. Assumption: the prototype's speed (117 cells in about 0.5 s) scales to 1.5–2k cells in 5–20 s.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: pgTAP runs in CI on every push. The matrix runs in CI and its red cells form the printed work list (E1–E5 all appear as red cells). A new *_service without a matrix row fails CI.

plan_steps.step: 2. Close the open surface. Everything here is a small migration or a deletion; no function logic is rewritten. Revoke execute by default in app_private, and revoke execute on its 3 functions that trust a caller-supplied user id. Revoke direct browser writes on workspace_memberships, membership_location_scopes, audit_events, workspace_onboarding and workspace_scheduling_settings, plus INSERT on workspaces and TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER everywhere. Allow UPDATE on workspaces only for the name and logo columns. Keep the grants the Settings > Organization screen really uses: it writes departments, jobs, locations, important_dates, shift_types, shift_labels and workspaces directly (checked in apps/web/src/settings/organization-data.ts). That contradicts investigation 1's claim that the web writes only 2 tables. Make the 9 single-column links composite FKs. Add the role FK (role_id, workspace_id, role) -> workspace_roles(id, workspace_id, access_class). Delete the dead and tautology policies and the dead legacy role functions. Gate the dev identity with one explicit flag that defaults to off. Move realtime to private channels with policies on realtime.messages. Fix the scheduled-export reads.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The catalog sweeps are green. Experiments E5, E6, E7, the workspaces lifecycle update and the fake audit insert, re-run as matrix rows or rolled-back probes, are now denied. Settings > Organization still saves (checked in the browser).

plan_steps.step: 3. Build the authorization core, designed once as a unit. app_private.actor_context(actor, workspace) resolves everything in one place: active membership (pending only for self-onboarding), workspace status, document block with an allowlist of actions still permitted, access_class from a single source, permissions from role data rather than a hard-coded employee list, and scope (all_locations for owner and admin only, otherwise derived locations). On top of it: authorize(actor, ws, action, target) returns or raises 42501 with a key in HINT; target kinds are workspace, location, location_set, person, shift, draft, request, self, document, announcement, notification and kiosk. scope_set(actor, ws, permission) returns the allowed location ids. A thin auth.uid() adapter serves the RLS policies that are deliberately kept. In the API, one authorize() in auth/workspace-context.ts replaces the 20 local helpers, and the 7 separate token-to-user resolvers collapse to one. Assumption: M2 is chosen. Under M1, M3 or M4 only the target rules change, not the structure.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The matrix's predicate-consistency layer is green for the core. The API route matrix is green. schedule-routes, lineup, requests and onboarding no longer have local gates.

plan_steps.step: 4. Route every check through the core, one domain at a time: schedule, employees, time off and exchanges, communication and important dates, settings, documents, then time and kiosk only where they are called. Each API-callable entry point calls authorize() first, before any payload validation. Replace the inline checks and the 45 functions that borrow the logged-in-user slot. Collapse a wrapper chain only when it is being touched. RPC signatures and output shapes stay as they are, so the web does not move. Assumption: AI writes the mechanical rewrites and the owner reviews; one domain per 2–4 days.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The matrix is green for each finished domain. Structural tests pass: 0 functions call set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub'); only actor_context reads membership_location_scopes or all_locations; every non-exempt actor *_service calls authorize(). Existing vitest and typecheck are green, showing no shape drift.

plan_steps.step: 5. The two contained model changes that authorize() cannot express today, plus the rules that sit next to them. (a) Plan-edit locks, sessions and drafts become per location plus week, and a save touches only the session's locations (G's D3 / HATA-2, data loss). (b) The time-off request loses its location_id; everyone who can see the person sees it, and approval takes a vote from each affected location (M2 D4). (c) D3 on terminate and archive; rank checks on time-off and swap approvals (D5). Assumption: no live data, so these are schema edits plus a fixture rebuild, with no data migration.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: G's scenarios S3 (two managers planning the same week), S5 (Ali's time off across two locations) and S8 (terminating Ali) are matrix or regression rows and are green. An admin taking over a session no longer deletes another location's shifts, re-run as a rolled-back probe.

plan_steps.step: 6. Fix the verified BL-070 bugs. Finish or delete a half-migration only where it blocks one of them. The fixes: the preferred-name wipe in save_employee_service; the manager-terminate regression; BL-091, where the grid's 4 live readers move to the new availability system and the old one is dropped with its tests; approved time off always hard, enforced by a CHECK and by removing that settings row; recipients for preferred-name notifications; BL-092, passing the exclusion list to the candidate evaluator; Shift Hub, either an enable path or the flag deleted, following the step 0 decision, and whichever of Shift Hub or the old Requests flow loses is deleted; an 'Employee view' route for owner, admin and manager in App.tsx. Then decide each of the 38 red files: fix it, rewrite it, or delete it.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Every item in the research README's 'heaviest findings' table has a test and is green. The 38 reds are resolved, except Line Up 32–38, which is explicitly parked. The CI allowlist becomes the whole suite minus Line Up.

plan_steps.step: 7. Test-harness debt, limited to what keeps the suite in step with decisions. Build one shared fixture builder that goes through product entry points and uses gen_random_uuid. Remove hand-inserted manager scopes from each file as it is touched. Replace the 106 per-function grant checks with the one catalog sweep. Delete the 9 vitest files that pattern-match migration text. Make the date-dependent files use a far-future relative week. Assumption: the untouched files that are already green can keep their fixtures until they are next edited.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The full pgTAP suite (minus Line Up) runs green in CI. A decision change is one line in expected(), and the matrix shows which cells it flips.

total_effort_range_weeks: 8.5–15 (sum of steps 0–7). A person-week means the owner directing, reviewing and deciding while AI writes code; the owner's decision time, not code generation, is the bottleneck. Assumptions: M2 is decided in step 0; Line Up, kiosk/time deletion and a migration squash are excluded; no data migration is needed. The security and CI value lands after steps 0–2, about 2–3.5 weeks. For comparison, the rebuild-cost investigation's estimates are 8–14 for a targeted option (which includes parallel-system deletion and a squash) and 13–24 for a full rebuild, and the full rebuild still has to build this same core, matrix and CI gate.
risks: Stopping halfway. Both authorization styles stay alive while domains are migrated one by one. This is exactly how the 2026-09-08 hardening ended up with 45 slot-borrowing bridges and 20 local API helpers. Mitigation: the structural tests in step 4 are exit criteria that fail CI, not intentions.

A wrong expected() is enforced faithfully. The matrix is only as right as the decisions behind it (M2, D1, D3, approved time off). If the owner changes the scope model later, the rules change but the structure stays.

Revoking grants can break screens. Settings > Organization writes 7 tables directly from the browser (departments, jobs, locations, important_dates, shift_types, shift_labels, workspaces), which contradicts investigation 1's '2 tables' claim. A blanket revoke would break that screen, so step 2 has to keep those grants or move the writes behind the API.

Output-shape drift. Routing checks through authorize() must not change what the RPCs return, or the 168 web files that read those shapes break silently where tests are thin. Typecheck plus vitest is the only guard.
Revokes lost on drop/recreate. This happened to apply_owner_onboarding_update. The catalog sweeps must cover app_private and every future schema, or the class of bug returns.
The routing step may overrun. 239 functions call helpers, 51 carry their own checks, and wrapper chains go 5 deep. The 2.5–4 week estimate for step 4 is the least certain number.
Running supabase start in CI adds minutes and possible flakiness. There is already one known intermittent test (the Line-up share test). An allowlist that only grows limits the damage.
The local database is shared with other sessions, and the FX leftover shows experiments can leak. Matrix fixtures must stay inside rollback-ended transactions.

Hosted facts were not verified: NODE_ENV on Vercel, which schemas the hosted project exposes, and whether hosted grants match local. Step 2's fixes should be checked against the hosted project with the security advisors after the push.

The surface stays larger because of what is kept: kiosk/time (14 tables), Line Up (11) and untouched wrapper layers stay, so authorize() and the matrix must cover or exempt code that may later be deleted anyway.
strongest_argument_against_self: This codebase has already tried consolidating in place, and it did not finish. The 2026-09-08 hardening (20260908132000) moved the product from 'browser calls PostgREST under RLS' to 'API calls service_role functions' one piece at a time. It left 39 auth.uid() functions, 45 functions bridging the two worlds by borrowing the logged-in-user slot, 8 dead policies, 28 still-granted tables and 20 local API gates. With 407 function rewrites across the migrations, drop-and-recreate repeatedly lost grants. The rebuild-cost investigation reads this as a foundation flaw that must be replaced 'as one designed unit, not refactored helper by helper'. Option A's safeguard is to design authorize() once, up front, and let CI fail while any old-style check survives. Even so, A keeps paying the costs a fresh baseline would drop. The kept parallel systems (kiosk/time, Line Up, old requests if not chosen) enlarge the surface authorize() and the matrix must cover. The 319-migration history, and the 36 _base layers in untouched areas, keep slowing every reader. And with no live data, the usual reason to prefer incremental change, protecting production data, does not exist here. A disciplined rebuild of just the authorization layer, plus a squash, might finish cleaner in similar time. What argues back is scale and precedent. Most of what a rebuild would replace is sound: about 110 domain tables, 4,275 decided assertions, and web shapes used in 168 files. And the one full rebuild so far, written with a brief that demanded these exact controls, reproduced the same failures within 5 weeks.

option: B: rebuild the authorization core on a clean foundation, one domain at a time (strangler)
thesis: This is not a dead end in the data model. It is a loop in one layer. The domain tables are sound: 191 of 202 tenant links are composite, RLS is on for 152 of 152 tables, the actor comes from the verified login token, and 0 functions that take an actor are callable from the browser. So neither a from-scratch rebuild nor a "Gen 4" is justified. The authorization layer, though, is an unfinished move between two architectures. On 2026-09-08 the design moved from "browser under RLS" to "API calls service functions", and the move stopped halfway. What is left: 45 functions that fake the JWT user so older auth.uid() code keeps working, 3 identity channels, 16 separate location-scope implementations that disagree, 20 route-local API gates, and a live third write path. On Settings > Organization the browser writes 7 tables directly, and the API has its own POST/PATCH for jobs and departments (verified this session). Access rules are also written by hand, function by function: 823 revoke lines and 441 grant-execute lines across 319 migrations. Dropping and recreating a function silently loses them, and that has happened at least twice (the app_private apply_owner_onboarding_update function, and a hosted function caught by the security advisor on 2026-09-22). This is why every fix feels like patching a hole. Each fix corrects one copy and its siblings drift: the manager-terminate regression of 2026-09-14, a document-blocked manager writing shifts (E1), and a manager archiving another location's draft through a NULL location (E2). Option B replaces that layer as one designed unit instead of refactoring it helper by helper. That helper-by-helper route is exactly what produced today's hybrid. The order is: 1. Decide the scope model (M2). 2. Put pgTAP in CI and build an authorization matrix whose single expected() function is the executable spec. 3. Delete the parallel systems that double every rule (old availability, the legacy Requests flow, kiosk and time tracking; of 158 tables ever created, none has been dropped). 4. Squash what is left into a fresh baseline, which is cheap because there is no live data. 5. Build one authorize() plus scope_set() with semantics decided once: NULL never means "anywhere", an empty set means org-wide, one way of saying "no", and it runs before validation. 6. Move domains over one at a time, each finished only when its matrix cells are green. What separates this from the failed Gen-3 rebuild (90f0fad, whose brief prescribed these same controls in writing) is order: the enforcement (matrix, CI gate, catalog tests) comes first, and the rebuild targets only the layer that is actually broken. Each step is shippable on its own. Stopping after step 3 already gives what Option A would give.
what_it_fixes: A document-blocked manager can still edit and publish schedules (E1). Actor checks happen once (membership status, workspace lifecycle, document block with an allowlist, role class, permissions), and the API and the database both use that one result.

A missing location counts as 'anywhere' in 4 helpers, and 56 call sites rely on it (E2: a Main Dining manager archived a Garden Room draft). authorize() never accepts NULL as 'anywhere', and scope_set() filters lists.

The 16 location-scope implementations and 6 'can this manager reach this person' implementations disagree on the document block, workspace lifecycle, role class, the ANY-location vs ALL-locations rule and empty sets. They are replaced by one predicate. A consistency check in the matrix proves it.

Direct browser writes that bypass the API are closed through a default-deny grant allowlist with a catalog test. Today an admin can mark the organization deleted or switch on Shift Hub, an admin can repoint a membership to another tenant's employee, an owner can widen a manager's scope outside the assignment rule (E5), and any employee can add backdated audit rows.
Grants lost on drop-and-recreate: catalog tests now cover every schema, including app_private (3 definer functions anyone can execute today), and every definer function, so a lost revoke fails CI.

Role stored twice: a composite foreign key from memberships (role_id, workspace_id, role) to the role's (id, workspace_id, access_class) makes drift impossible. The employee permission allowlist (4 copies today) and the role defaults (3 copies) move to one SQL source.
The 11 single-column links without workspace_id become composite, so a cross-tenant link can no longer be written.

The plan-edit lock is one per workspace and week, so taking over a session wipes another location's draft. The lock becomes per location and week, and save only touches the session's own locations (M2 D3). Drafts and sessions carry their location set so authorize() can express the rule.
The Schedule grid reads the old availability system while save and publish use the new one. The old system is deleted after its 4 live readers are moved over.
Shift Hub is switched off everywhere and the legacy Requests flow runs in parallel. After this there is one exchange system, with an enable path and manager approval.
Approved time off can be softened in Settings. A database CHECK makes it always hard, and the settings row is removed.

Managers cannot terminate (the 2026-09-14 regression), D3 is not enforced, and there is no rank check on approvals. These become rules inside authorize(): all of the person's locations in scope, and a manager acts only on employee rank.

Bugs from stacked wrapper functions: saving an employee wipes the approved preferred name, and a swap counts the given-up shift as a conflict with itself (BL-092). The wrapper chains collapse to one function, and the command is checked at the entry point.
20 route-local API gates, 7 of which skip the document-restriction check, plus 7 separate token-to-user resolvers, become one exported API authorize().
Dev identity bypasses, dead fallback paths, public live-update channels (made private) and the scheduled export that reads tables its role cannot read are all fixed.

Tests stop falling out of step with decisions. A decision changes one line of expected(), and the run lists exactly which cells flip. Manager fixtures are created through the product's own path instead of hand-inserted scope rows (57 of 59 manager files today). pgTAP gates CI.
The migration history becomes readable: one baseline instead of 407 function rewrites, taken after the deletions so it does not carry the dead systems.
what_it_does_not_fix: Product decisions still have to be made: the scope model (M2 or another), whether old availability goes (BL-091), Shift Hub vs legacy Requests, how owner, admin and manager reach their own shifts, and what happens to kiosk and time tracking. B only gives each answer one place to land.

Web gating. The Employee Hub route is limited to roles=['employee'], and the web has 64 permission checks and 10 route guards. The matrix cannot see these unless the web later adopts a single can(action) helper that is checked against the matrix's exported expectations.
Eligibility for swap, cover and release (location + job + availability). That needs a second matrix on the same engine. authorize() answers who may act, not who is eligible to take a shift.
Preferred-name notifications that go nowhere (no recipient list) and notification recipients in general (BL-099).
Fields leaking inside an allowed response, for example private contact details.
Line Up (11 tables, 7 red files). It is deliberately excluded and waits for its own simplification decision.
Web size and coupling: 85k lines, 3,495 snake_case field reads in 168 files. B keeps RPC output shapes stable on purpose, so this coupling stays.
The working method itself. AI agents will still re-implement a rule unless the coverage sweep and catalog tests reject it. B makes the drift visible, but someone still has to keep the gates on.
Feature progress during the program. The MVP pauses for about 2.5 to 4 months.

plan_steps.step: 0. Decide before building. The owner settles the questions the whole program depends on: scope model M2 ('person shared, shift local', per G), removing the old availability system (BL-091), one exchange system (Shift Hub), deleting kiosk and time tracking (outside the MVP and forbidden by the Gen-3 rebuild brief), an employee view for owner, admin and manager, approved time off always hard, and Line Up excluded. ASSUMPTION: the owner accepts G's recommendations or answers within the week. Every open question later becomes a 'decide:' todo cell instead of blocking work.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The decision list is written in the project conventions file. Each of G's D1-D7 is marked accepted, changed or deferred. The scope sentence in the target-model text is rewritten to match.

plan_steps.step: 1. Put the gate in place, plus security stopgaps. Add a CI job that runs supabase start and pgTAP over an explicit list of green files, which may only grow. Widen the catalog guard tests to public plus app_private and to every definer function. Remove execute-by-anyone from the 3 app_private definer functions and fix app_private default privileges. Delete the dev-token bypass in workspace-account-service and the dead development and fallback routes. Revoke the unused browser write grants (memberships, scope rows, audit_events, workspaces INSERT, workspace_onboarding, workspace_scheduling_settings, TRUNCATE). Limit browser UPDATE on workspaces to name and logo. Leave the 7 Settings > Organization tables writable until step 5. ASSUMPTION: each item is a small migration pushed to hosted with the linked CLI, followed by the security advisor check.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: CI fails when a listed pgTAP file regresses. Tables the browser can write = the 7 Settings > Organization tables + user_profiles + user_preferences. Re-running the membership-repoint, scope-insert (E5) and workspace-lifecycle experiments in rolled-back sessions returns a denial. Hosted security advisors show no new issues.

plan_steps.step: 2. Fixture builder + authorization matrix (the executable spec). One builder creates worlds through the product's own entry points, uses fresh random ids, forces deferred triggers to run (set constraints all immediate), and gives managers their scope only through their own location assignments. Add authorization_matrix.test.sql: 14 actors (owner, admin, managers at Kadıköy, at Beşiktaş, at both, and at no location, a narrowed custom role, employees with one and with two locations, suspended, pending, removed, another tenant) × about 45 actions × 8 target kinds, plus reads of the 28 browser-granted tables. pg_temp.expected() is the only place decisions live. Each cell is probed and undone with a sentinel exception. A consistency layer checks that all location predicates agree. A coverage sweep requires every *_service function that takes an actor to be in authz_action or in authz_exempt with a reason. ASSUMPTION: the 117-cell prototype (about 0.5 s) scales to about 1,500-2,000 cells in 5-20 s (extrapolated, not measured).
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The matrix runs in CI. Today's known divergences (E1-E5, NULL location, D3 terminate, the four different ways of saying no) show as listed failing cells, not silenced ones. Open questions print as todo cells. A new service function that takes an actor fails CI until its rule is recorded.

plan_steps.step: 3. Delete the parallel and legacy systems. Old availability: 8 tables and about 74 functions; move its 4 live readers first, including the Schedule grid's read model, to weekly preferences. Legacy Requests shift-change flow: 3 tables; keep Shift Hub, add its enable path, drop the flag. Kiosk (6 tables) and time tracking (8). Also: tombstone functions, _v2/_v3 duplicates, the ~20-30 functions nobody calls, the 8 dead RLS policies and the tautology policies, duplicate settings columns kept in sync by a trigger, the bl051 snapshot tables, the 'unknown shift time' states, and the pgTAP files that describe retired models. ASSUMPTION: no live data, so deleting needs no data migration. The rebuild inventory estimates this work as risky, mainly because of the grid read-model port.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Nothing reads employee_schedule_availability_versions any more. The grid, save and publish all read one availability system. About 25-30 fewer tables. CI's green list and the matrix stay green, apart from cells that were already failing.

plan_steps.step: 4. Squash to a fresh baseline. Take a schema-only dump of the post-deletion schema as one baseline migration. Rebuild seed.sql and the Meyhouse fixture through the builder. Reset the hosted project and repair its migration history. ASSUMPTION: hosted data can be thrown away (2 workspaces and 3 employees as of 2026-09-22) and the CLI link works. Note: a baseline taken before deletions would still be about 54.8k lines against 66.8k lines of migrations, which is why it comes after step 3.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: A from-zero local reset (baseline + later migrations) passes the catalog tests and the matrix. Hosted `db push --dry-run` reports up to date. The hosted security advisor is clean.

plan_steps.step: 5. The authorization core. SQL: authorize(actor, workspace, action, target) and scope_set(actor, workspace, permission). Actor checks run once. Role class comes from one source: the composite foreign key makes membership.role a projection the database enforces. Permissions come from role data, with no hard-coded employee list. Owner and admin see all locations; everyone else gets locations derived from their own assignments. Target kinds: workspace, location, location set (ALL rule; empty = org-wide), person (ANY rule to read and for person-only edits; ALL rule or per-location votes for cross-location effects; rank rule), shift, draft or session (its location set), request, self, document, announcement, notification. There is one denial, 42501 with a machine key in HINT, raised before validation. API: one exported authorize() in auth/workspace-context.ts and one token resolver, replacing the 20 local helpers and 7 resolvers. Browser: move the 7 Settings > Organization writes behind the existing API routes (jobs and departments routes already exist), so browser grants shrink to the user's own rows and read-only catalogs. The few remaining policies call authorize(auth.uid(), ...). Make the realtime channels private. ASSUMPTION: 'policies regenerated from a declared matrix' collapses into a grant-allowlist catalog test. Once almost nothing is directly granted, a policy generator would be over-engineering.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: The predicate-consistency layer is green, including NULL-location cells. An API route matrix is green (restricted, suspended, employee and wrong-workspace contexts across every route). The catalog test enforces the allowlist of browser-granted tables. The important_dates read respects location.

plan_steps.step: 6. Move domains over one at a time (strangler), including M2 D1-D7. Order by risk: (a) Schedule: per-location and per-week lock, save touches only the session's own locations, drafts carry their location set, the conflict check sees other locations' published shifts, and those shifts appear as grey read-only blocks on the grid. (b) People: terminate and archive under D3, the rank rule, the restored manager terminate, the 11 composite FKs, the preferred-name wipe. (c) Time off: drop location_id, per-affected-location votes, approved time off enforced as hard by a CHECK. (d) Exchanges: rank check (D5), BL-092 exclusion, manager approval. (e) Availability and preferences. (f) Documents and onboarding. (g) Announcements, important dates, notifications. (h) Settings, account, workspace lifecycle. For each domain: every entry point calls authorize() first, wrapper chains collapse, the fake-JWT wrappers are removed, RPC output shapes stay the same, the domain's pgTAP files move onto the builder, and per-function grant assertions are deleted. ASSUMPTION: stable RPC shapes limit web changes to the intended UI changes (grey blocks, a time-off form with no location, the employee view switch, Shift Hub enable). Budget covers M2 D1-D7 (1.5-3 weeks per G and the inventory) plus wrapper collapse.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Per domain: its matrix cells are green with no 'decide' left, it has no fake-JWT wrappers, no inline scope logic (a catalog regex test), and its red files are resolved. For the whole program: fake-JWT bridges 45 to 0, location-scope implementations 16 to 1, route-local API gates 20 to 0, coverage sweep complete, the 31 red files outside Line Up resolved or deleted.

total_effort_range_weeks: 10-17. Assumptions: a week is the owner directing, reviewing and deciding, since AI code generation is not the bottleneck; M2 is decided in step 0; Line Up is excluded; there is no data migration; RPC output shapes stay stable. The rebuild inventory's own 'targeted option' came to 8-14 weeks. This range is higher because the fixture builder, the security stopgaps and the hosted reset are counted separately. Stopping after step 2 (about 2.5-4 weeks) already delivers what Option A would.
risks: It turns into a second-system effect. The repo already is a rebuild (90f0fad, 2026-08-18), and within 5 weeks it recreated the defects its own brief forbade. A multi-month 'clean foundation' program is the same temptation. Mitigation: gates first, only the authorization layer is rebuilt, the domain tables stay, and the program can stop cleanly after any step.

It stops halfway and leaves three authorization styles instead of two. That is exactly how today's state arose after the 2026-09-08 hardening. Mitigation: the coverage sweep and catalog regex tests fail CI while any domain is still on the old helpers, and each domain is finished before the next starts.

The owner's decision bandwidth is the real bottleneck. 58% of all migration lines were written in 3 days (Sep 7-9), while decisions take weeks. If step 0 questions stay open, cells stay 'decide' and the domain moves stall.
The estimate overruns. The grid read-model port (old availability) and time-off per-location votes are the riskiest pieces; both are shared rules that fail quietly.

Squash and hosted reset mechanics. A dump-derived baseline can carry wrong default ACLs, and dropping a function drops its grants. It is only safe once the all-schema catalog tests and the matrix pass on a from-zero DB, and the hosted advisor is run afterwards.

Coverage lost while rewriting tests. There are 4,275 assertions today. The matrix replaces about 300-350 authorization assertions plus 106 grant checks, but the 80-120 non-authorization ones (lease theft, spoofing, idempotency, response-shape leaks) must be kept deliberately, not swept away.
Changing how the system says 'no' may break web error handling. Screens that expect NULL, empty or not-found (P0002) today will receive 42501. Each domain move must check its screens.
Settings > Organization would break if browser grants are revoked before its 7 direct writes move behind the API. The steps are ordered to avoid this, but it is easy to get wrong.
The expected() function encodes a wrong decision just as faithfully as a right one. It is visible in one place, but still wrong until someone reads it.
Shared local database and parallel sessions. Long programs make it more likely that a migration or fixture change collides with another session's work.
strongest_argument_against_self: Four of the six investigations, and the coworker, independently concluded that consolidating in place is enough. The core identity pattern is sound, and every security finding's fix is 'one small migration or a deletion' (investigations 1, 3, 4). Investigation 4 shows even role duplication closes with 2 lines of DDL and no function rewrites. The only things that would actually have stopped the regressions are the authorization matrix, pgTAP in CI and the catalog tests, and Option A includes all three at about 2-3.5 weeks. Most of what B adds on top (the squash, the policy regeneration, a committed domain-by-domain move of everything) buys readability and uniformity, not correctness a user would notice. A pre-deletion baseline would still be 54,845 lines against 66,827. Meanwhile the MVP pauses for 2.5-4 months. The repo's own history cuts against B: Gen 3 was exactly a 'build a correct foundation and build on it' program, with a written brief demanding location scope in every check, no SECURITY DEFINER shortcuts and role test users. It rebuilt the same failure classes within 5 weeks. A program shaped like B risks becoming the next half-finished migration. A could ship the security fixes in week 1 and the data-losing lock fix in week 2, then consolidate as domains are touched. That is B without the commitment, the pause, or the risk of stopping midway with three authorization styles.

option: C: Full rebuild from scratch. Design a new database, RLS, policy and backend foundation from zero on the M2 model, then rebuild the API and adapt the web app on top of it. Shape it as a gated rebuild that keeps the web contract: tests and CI checks come before any domain table, and the packages/shared response shapes stay fixed wherever M2 does not change the domain.
thesis:
The honest case for C is narrower than "the foundation is broken". It rests on three measured facts:

1. There is no live data. The usual main cost of a rebuild (moving data, running two systems side by side) is zero.

2. The targeted alternative already rewrites most of the function layer. Its steps are: one authorize() at depth 0 in every entry point, rewriting the 45 functions that fake the logged-in user, collapsing the _base wrapper layers, deleting 36 half-finished parallel tables, squashing 319 migrations into one baseline, and rebuilding the test fixtures. A rolled-back catalog query found that 426 of 718 functions (18,881 of 26,625 function-body lines, about 71%) match the authorization, wrapper-layer or parallel-system patterns. That is a heuristic upper bound. On top of that, the test harness has to be largely rewritten either way: 57 of the 59 files that create a manager test a manager the product cannot actually create, the tests contain 1,242 hand-written inserts, and 34% of expected-error checks pin exact message wording. So the real gap between "targeted" and "full" is mostly re-typing the ~110 domain tables that are sound, plus re-checking behaviour already decided in the areas that work today. It is not a gap between "patch" and "rewrite".

3. The main argument against C is that the last rebuild failed within 5 weeks. But that rebuild (Gen 3) was never a gated rebuild:
- Its first commit (90f0fad) imported 69,757 lines in 246 files, including 8 kiosk and time-tracking migrations that its own brief forbade.
- The first CI workflow arrived four weeks later (77d5c38, 2026-09-16), and it has never run the database tests.
- There were 12 commits in the first three weeks.
So Gen 3 disproves "an ungated port", not "a rebuild whose tests and CI checks exist before its code".

Built that way (decisions frozen first, the authorization matrix and catalog tests red in CI before any domain table, M2 designed into the schema), C produces a foundation with:
- exactly one authorization style
- zero direct browser write grants
- manager location scope derived by a view, not by deferred sync triggers
- per-location plan-edit locks
- time off without a location
- no leftover layers
The targeted option reaches the same end state by surgery on a 55k-line schema with 407 historical function rewrites, where a drop-and-recreate has already silently lost a permission revoke once.

C costs about 13–22 person-weeks against 8–14 for the targeted option. It is the right choice only if the owner values a foundation they can fully reason about over roughly 5–8 weeks of MVP time. That is a real trade, not a clear win.
what_it_fixes: Two authorization styles, which is the foundation-level flaw: 284 functions take the acting user as a parameter, 39 read the logged-in user from the session instead, and 45 functions bridge the two by overwriting the logged-in user id mid-transaction. C replaces all of this with one style: the API verifies the login and passes the actor to one authorize(actor, workspace, action, target) plus a scope_set() used by listings. There is no user-id faking in any function

The location rule is written 12 times at helper level, 6 more times for 'can the manager reach this person', inline in 51 functions, and in 20 API route helpers, and the copies disagree. Examples: an empty location counts as 'anywhere' in 4 helpers; a document-blocked manager can still write a shift; a suspended workspace still accepts direct edits to its locations. In C every rule is decided once, and empty-set and empty-location handling is defined once

Direct browser writes: 15 tables are writable straight from the browser, but the web app writes only 2. The rest let an admin mark the organization deleted, switch on Shift Hub, re-point a membership to another company's employee record, fake audit-log entries, or widen a manager's locations. C starts with zero browser write grants except user_profiles and user_preferences, and a catalog test enforces that

Default-deny across every schema from the first migration. This closes the internal schema (app_private) gap where 3 internal functions that trust a caller-supplied user id are executable by everyone, and the lost revoke on apply_owner_onboarding_update

The data-losing plan-edit lock: today there is one lock per workspace and week. In C, drafts, locks and edit sessions are scoped per location, so an admin's takeover can no longer wipe another location's draft shifts

The M2 domain designed in from the start: time off belongs to the person (no location field), approval is a vote per affected location, the rank rule applies to approvals, and the 'every one of the person's locations' rule applies to terminate and archive
Approved time off is always a hard conflict, enforced by a database constraint, so no setting can soften it
Role stored once: the role label is tied to the role's access class by a foreign key or generated column, so the two can never disagree
Employee permission limits and role defaults kept in one data source instead of 4 and 3 copies

Manager location scope as a view over the manager's own location assignments. This removes the 17 deferred triggers that never fire in tests, and fixtures can no longer fake a manager scope the product would erase
All 11 tenant-to-tenant links carry the workspace, with no exceptions

The 36 parallel or half-finished tables are simply not rebuilt: old availability (8), legacy shift-change requests (3), kiosk (6), time tracking (8) and Line Up (11, pending its own decision). This also removes the root of the Schedule grid reading the old availability system while save and publish use the new one

No wrapper layers: 36 _base wrappers, up to 5 deep, go away, along with 3 tombstone functions, 11 _v2/_v3 duplicates and duplicate settings columns. The preferred-name wipe on employee save and BL-092 (a swap counting the given-up shift as a conflict with itself) both came from these layers

One way to say 'no': permission code 42501 plus a machine-readable reason key, checked before input validation. Today there are 195 different messages, some denials come back as NULL, and some as 'employee not found'

Test harness built right from day one: fixtures created through the product's own entry points, generated ids, no dependence on seed.sql, the authorization matrix as the written specification, a coverage sweep that fails when a new entry point has no recorded rule, and pgTAP as a required CI check
A clean migration history: one designed baseline instead of 319 migrations, 407 function rewrites and 0 tables ever dropped
The dev-login bypass and the fallback login paths are deleted, not gated. Realtime channels are private and protected by policies
Owner, admin and manager can reach the employee screens (for their own shifts, time off and swaps), and Shift Hub is switched on by product decision instead of a flag with no screen
what_it_does_not_fix: Open product decisions. The rebuild cannot start until they are made, and it does not make them: the M2 edge cases, Line Up simplification, D1–D3, Shift Hub vs the legacy Requests flow, and BL-091

Whether decisions actually get enforced. Gen 3 had a written brief with these exact rules (C:/Users/TheWe/newfork/docs/clean-rebuild-ai-handoff/06-technology-and-architecture.md) and ignored it. Only the tests and CI checks prevent drift, and the targeted option can have the same ones

The identity core. Checking the login on the server and passing the actor to service functions already works everywhere (135 call sites, 0 browser-callable functions that trust a supplied user id). A rebuild would produce the same thing, so there is no gain here
The screen-level and API-level permission checks written in TypeScript (64 checks in the web app, 31 in the API) are not covered by a database matrix unless a separate web/API test is written
Eligibility (location + job + availability), notification recipients, and lock/concurrency data loss. These need their own test grids beyond the authorization matrix
Visible features stall for most of the rebuild. There are no live users, so no customer is hurt, but the MVP date slips
A rebuild does not make AI agents follow the backlog, the conventions file or the decision records. That is a process problem, and it caused the Gen 3 drift

plan_steps.step: 0. Freeze decisions before any code. Decide in writing: M2 ('person shared, shift local'), including D3 (a manager terminates or archives only if all of the person's locations are in their scope); BL-091 (new weekly availability only); Shift Hub replaces the legacy Requests flow; Line Up, kiosk and time tracking are excluded from the rebuild, and any of them re-enters only through the new tests and checks; approved time off is always hard; D1/D2 settings permissions; owner, admin and manager get an employee view. Assumption: the owner can answer G's questions 1–7 and README questions 1–5 in a few sittings.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: A single decision list exists where each decision maps to one line of the matrix expectation function. No open 'decide:' cell remains for anything inside the rebuild's scope.

plan_steps.step: 1. Build the tests and CI checks first, on an empty new baseline (a fresh migration baseline on a branch; the old main stays frozen as the reference; no data to migrate). Contents: a CI job that starts Supabase and runs pgTAP; catalog tests over every schema (no SECURITY DEFINER function executable by PUBLIC, anon or authenticated except an allowlist; default privileges revoked in every schema; a table-grant allowlist; composite foreign keys on every tenant-to-tenant link; no faking of the logged-in user id; every service function that takes an actor calls authorize() at depth 0); a fixture builder that goes through product entry points with generated ids; and the authorization matrix harness (the probe-with-sentinel approach already prototyped at 117 cells in about 0.5 s). It covers 14 actors x ~45 actions x 8 target kinds, and the expected() function is built from step 0. Assumption: the prototype scripts in the scratchpad testinfra folder can be adapted rather than written anew.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: CI runs pgTAP on every push. Catalog tests pass on the empty baseline. The matrix is present and red, because no entry points exist yet. A deliberately planted violation (a PUBLIC-executable definer function, a direct write grant) turns CI red.

plan_steps.step: 2. Identity and authorization core. Tables: workspaces, memberships (role tied by composite foreign key to the role's access class), roles and permissions (an employee_eligible column and default role classes as data), employee_profiles, location and job assignments, and manager scope as a view over the manager's own assignments. Functions: authorize() and scope_set(), which resolve once: active membership, workspace lifecycle, document block with an allowlist of actions still permitted, access class, permissions, and scope. Denials are 42501 plus a reason key, checked before validation. API side: one token resolver, one authorize() gate, and a dev identity that is opt-in only.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Matrix cells for workspace, settings, person and role actions are green across active, pending, suspended, document-blocked and suspended-workspace states. The location-check consistency layer is green, including the empty-location case. Catalog tests stay green.

plan_steps.step: 3. Rebuild the domain in vertical slices against M2. The current class-1 table definitions and business logic serve as reference specs only; no wrapper chain is copied. Slices, in order: (a) org settings (locations, departments, jobs, shift types, labels, important dates), served through the API only; (b) employees, invitations, onboarding and documents; (c) schedule: shifts, per-location drafts, locks and edit sessions, publish, conflicts with approved time off as a constraint, and the new availability only; (d) time off without a location, with per-affected-location votes; (e) Shift Hub swap, cover and release, with an eligibility grid (location + job + availability, plus the self-override on pickup) and approval by both locations; (f) notifications with explicit recipients; (g) exports. Assumptions: class-3 systems stay out; AI generation is fast; the bottleneck is owner review and decisions.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: For each slice, its matrix cells and eligibility grid are green. Round-trip tests pass (save then read keeps the preferred name; a swap does not conflict with its own given-up shift; saving a draft touches only the session's locations). No entry point is deeper than one function below authorize(). The coverage sweep reports 100%.

plan_steps.step: 4. Rewire the API: point the 288 routes at the new service functions. Keep the packages/shared zod response shapes wherever M2 did not change the domain, and change the contract only where the model changed (time-off location, per-location drafts, vote status). Delete the 20 local authorize helpers and the 7 separate token resolvers. Assumption: most response shapes survive, so the change stays mostly inside the service modules.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: API vitest is green. A route-matrix test passes that runs every route with an employee context, a restricted (document-blocked) context and a suspended context. No route reads identity from the request body or ordinary headers.

plan_steps.step: 5. Adapt the web app. Update the data modules where contracts changed. Remove direct Supabase table reads except user_profiles and user_preferences. Add the employee view for owner, admin and manager. Remove the screens for excluded systems. Assumption: a large share of the 3,495 snake_case field reads stay valid because the shapes were kept.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Web typecheck, lint and tests are green. A manual tour of the main screens (Schedule, Employees, Time Off, Shift Hub, Settings) passes with owner, admin, manager (two locations) and employee fixture accounts, and matches the matrix.

plan_steps.step: 6. Stabilise and cut over. Replace main with the rebuilt branch, rebuild the local fixture and the hosted database (no data to keep), run the Supabase security advisors, and make a separate, gated decision on whether Line Up, kiosk or time tracking come back.
plan_steps.exit_criteria: Main CI is green with pgTAP included. The security advisors show no findings. Two weeks of normal work add no new red test files. The old main is tagged as the reference and its worktrees are closed.

total_effort_range_weeks: 13-22 (person-weeks of owner directing, reviewing and deciding while AI agents write the code; assumes M2 is decided first, Line Up, kiosk and time tracking are excluded, and no data migration is needed. The targeted option is 8-14 on the same assumptions)
risks: It becomes a second-system rebuild (Gen 4). Gen 3 drifted in 5 weeks. If the step-1 tests and CI checks slip, or domain code arrives in large imports as it did in 90f0fad, C reproduces the same failures at a higher cost. Mitigation: a hard stop rule that no domain migration merges without its matrix cells

Behaviour that was already decided gets lost. Existing checks encode decisions: 4,275 pgTAP assertions, 2,062 unit tests, 48 plan tasks, 63 backlog items and 24 decision memories. Areas that work today (document lifecycle, notification outbox, the publish flow, two-location swap voting) can regress because they are re-derived rather than kept
The MVP slips about 5-8 weeks beyond the targeted option, and there is no visible product progress during steps 1-3
The web contract drifts. If response shapes are not held fixed, the web rework spreads across 168 files and 3,495 field reads, and the web estimate doubles
Decisions change mid-rebuild (M2 edge cases, Line Up) and cause rework in the slices

The estimate is uncertain. The ranges are extrapolated from one inventory and one matrix prototype, not from a measured rebuilt slice. The first slice (org settings) should be timed and the plan re-estimated

Freezing main means real bugs in the current code (the data-losing plan-edit lock, the preferred-name wipe) stay unfixed for months unless they are hot-fixed on the old main, which creates two lines of code to keep in step
The owner's decision capacity is the true bottleneck. A rebuild asks for more of it than the targeted option does
strongest_argument_against_self:
This repo already is a full rebuild, and its brief prescribed exactly the controls now missing: tenant and location scope in every check, no SECURITY DEFINER shortcuts, owner/admin/manager/employee test users, and no kiosk or time tracking. The same failure classes came back within 5 weeks.

All six investigations independently found the same things. The domain model (about 110 tables, 191 of 202 tenant links composite, RLS on everywhere) is sound. The identity core is what a rebuild would produce again. No BL-070 defect needs a different domain model.

The targeted option gets the same end state: the same authorize(), the same matrix, the same CI gate, the same deletions and the same squashed baseline. It costs 8-14 weeks instead of 13-22, and it keeps behaviour that is already decided and working.

My main counter is that Gen 3 was an ungated port, not a gated rebuild. That is true, but it cuts both ways. If the tests and CI checks are what actually prevents drift, the targeted option gets them too, and it gets them sooner. So C's extra 5-8 weeks mostly pay for re-typing sound tables and re-deriving decided behaviour.

The honest conclusion: C is justified only if the owner explicitly prefers a foundation they designed end-to-end over MVP time, or if the M2 decision ends up changing the domain's shape more than G's D1-D7 list suggests.
